prompt.context: Your client, NASA, has recently learned of a giant asteroid heading towards the Earth. Scientists at NASA have determined that there is a 10 percent probability that this asteroid makes landfall. If it hits, the asteroid will create a large dust storm blocking out sunlight and preventing photosynthesis in plants. This will ultimately destroy the rest of the earth's ecosystem for the next 100 years. NASA needs help determining whether they should launch the Eternity Mission, a space exploration mission to find a suitable planet for the human population to live on in the event of the catastrophic asteroid impact.
prompt.question: Should NASA launch the Eternity Mission? If so, which planet should they explore first?

clarifying_info.q: What is NASA's goal if the asteroid hits?
clarifying_info.a: NASA's goal is to safely evacuate at least 20% of the world's population in the event of impact.

clarifying_info.q: How much time does NASA have?
clarifying_info.a: The asteroid would hit earth in 25 years. NASA estimates it will require 15 years to build enough space vehicles and safely evacuate 20% of the world's population. Therefore, Mission Eternity needs to be completed within 10 years.
Assume NASA has had major breakthroughs in space travel and spacecraft can now travel at the speed of light.

clarifying_info.q: Can other space agencies contribute budget?
clarifying_info.a: Other international space agencies are looking to NASA to make a decision. Their budgets are unavailable to aid this mission.

NASA has already weighed other options to salvage the earth's population, such as hitting the asteroid to break it into smaller pieces, and determined that is not possible. Additionally, other efforts to live underground are being researched separately.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost of the mission?
clarifying_info.a: Cost of the Eternity Mission will vary by planet(s) selected for exploration; we do not have specific figures.

clarifying_info.q: How will astronauts survive such a long journey?
clarifying_info.a: Assume NASA has figured out a way to use therapeutic hypothermia hibernation to enable humans to travel very long distances in space.

framework: Budget Issues: cost of spacecraft, fuel (renewable technology), astronaut salaries/life insurance/family support/training, ground staff, tracking device upkeep, test runs; note outside fundraising (business, nonprofit, donations) is possible
Timing Issues: distance to each candidate planet, duration of project affects cost, timing of receiving planet data relative to the asteroid impact deadline
Public Relations / Liability: public response to expense, public reaction if mission accident occurs, loss of credibility for future missions if failure
Available Planet Data: accuracy of current data on potential planets, determining which metrics to prioritize for habitability

questions.prompt: Given the 10-year mission window, which planets can feasibly return data in time? Use Exhibit 1 to calculate total mission time for each planet.
questions.guidance: Candidate should convert trillion-mile distances to light years (1 light year = 6 trillion miles), add 18 months (1.5 years) for on-site data collection, then add signal return time (3 months per light year = 0.25 years per light year of distance). Planet W exceeds the 10-year deadline and should be eliminated. Strong candidates may shortcut: Planet X at 4 light years is clearly safe; Planet W at 8 light years + 1.5 + 2 = 11.5 clearly fails.

math.setup: Distance in light years = distance in trillion miles / 6. Signal return time (years) = distance in light years × (3 months / 12 months) = distance_ly × 0.25. Total time = travel time (light years) + data collection (1.5 years) + signal return time.
steps: Planet W: 48 / 6 = 8 LY travel; signal = 8 × 0.25 = 2 years; total = 8 + 1.5 + 2 = 11.5 years → EXCEEDS 10-year window, eliminate
Planet X: 24 / 6 = 4 LY travel; signal = 4 × 0.25 = 1 year; total = 4 + 1.5 + 1 = 6.5 years → feasible
Planet Y: 36 / 6 = 6 LY travel; signal = 6 × 0.25 = 1.5 years; total = 6 + 1.5 + 1.5 = 9 years → feasible
Planet Z: 33 / 6 = 5.5 LY travel; signal = 5.5 × 0.25 = 1.375 years; total = 5.5 + 1.5 + 1.375 = 8.375 years → feasible
math.answer: Planet W is eliminated (11.5 years > 10). Planets X (6.5 yr), Z (8.375 yr), and Y (9 yr) all return data within the 10-year window.

questions.prompt: Brainstorm: What metrics should NASA use to determine which of the remaining planets (X, Y, Z) to explore first?
questions.guidance: Candidate should organize ideas into buckets. Strong answers cover at least 4–5 categories with specific sub-items. Should ask for available data after brainstorming.

questions.prompt: NASA can only visit one planet. Using Exhibit 2, which planet should NASA explore?
questions.guidance: Candidate should read the scatter plot axes carefully. Planet Y has the highest ESI (~0.8) and the highest habitable zone percentile (~80th), making it the dominant choice. Candidate should ask for explanation of ESI and habitable zone if unfamiliar. Should note Planet Z as a potential secondary mission if budget allows.

brainstorming.prompt: How should NASA determine which planet to explore first? What metrics would you want to look at when comparing Planets X, Y, and Z?

categories.name: Distance from Earth
ideas: Feasibility of transferring population with less risk
Space travel timing — closer planet returns data sooner and leaves more build time

categories.name: Food and Water
ideas: Ability to raise livestock and sources of protein

categories.name: Atmospheric Conditions
ideas: Air quality — is it breathable without equipment?

categories.name: Natural Resources
ideas: Geography — buildable terrain, safety of terrain

recommendation: NASA should launch the Eternity Mission to Planet Y because it will return data before the 10-year deadline (9 years total) and has the highest indicators to sustain human life — an ESI of approximately 0.8 and a location in the 80th percentile of its habitable zone.
Given the 10% probability of impact, NASA must be budget-conscious, but the existential stakes justify proceeding with the mission.
risks: Planet Y is the furthest of the feasible planets from Earth, making the astronaut journey and hibernation riskier
The mission is more costly and represents a higher proportion of NASA's annual budget
There is a 90% probability the asteroid misses, making any expenditure a sunk cost if impact does not occur
Only one planet can be visited, so if Planet Y proves unsuitable there is no fallback mission time for the others
next_steps: Prepare and launch the Eternity Mission to Planet Y
Depending on available budget, consider launching a concurrent or follow-on mission to Planet Z (8.375 years), which also falls within the deadline and has moderate habitability indicators
Continue ground-level contingency planning (underground habitation research) in parallel
